newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan passes unpopular tax-raising budget.
newsitem.headline: Japan passes unpopular tax-raising budget.

text.p: Japan passed a tight state budget on Friday that has been touted as the start of a crackdown on government debt but criticised for raising taxes and doing little to help economic recovery.
The 1997/98 budget won approval from Japan's Upper House, passing into law with only a few days to go before the start of the new fiscal year and the unpopular rise in Japan's sales tax on April 1.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has billed the budget as the start of a belt-tightening exercise needed to cut Japan's ballooning state debt. Totalling 77.39 trillion yen ($629 billion), the budget is only three percent bigger than the previous year's original budget -- a relatively modest growth.
But analysts have said the package makes only half-hearted attempts to tackle the debt problem and fails to nurture the nation's still-fragile economic recovery.

Although the government insists it shows fiscal restraint, the budget has attracted much criticism for failing to drastically cut spending while tightening the screws on taxpayers by ending special income tax cuts and raising the consumption tax to five percent from three percent.
Although still low compared with other industrialised countries, the sales tax increase is bitterly resented by consumers. The sales tax, introduced in 1989, has not been raised until now.

The budget also set aside funds to study extending lines for Shinkansen bullet trains, heralding possible huge spending in the future. Critics said it showed inflexibility in perpetuating heavy spending on public works projects.
Economists say it is a tight budget that could do more harm than good to the economy.

Hisashi Yamada, an economist at Japan Research Institute, said: "We're running under tight fiscal finances. For example, public works investments fell by around two trillion yen ($16.2 billion) from last year. These things will inevitably work as a negative factor for the economy."
But economists said that with the recovery becoming more solid due to the strength of the private sector and external demand, there will be only a limited impact.

"Fiscal measures no longer play a major role in the economy. It's wrong to just look at the fiscal side and think that tighter finances would be bad for the economy," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities Japan Ltd.
"There's hardly any risk of the Japanese economy falling into recession again, although the growth may slow down (temporarily)," Kato said.

Hashimoto pledged last week to cut general spending in the state budget in the fiscal year starting in April 1998 from the previous year, as a way to reduce the state deficit to three percent of annual gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is seen at around 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, one of the worst levels among major industrialised countries.

Economists said the government's role now ought to be to help foster the budding strength in the private sector through deregulation, rather than reverting to the traditional remedy of public works projects to support economic growth.

Earlier on Friday, the government finalised a three-year programme to deregulate the economy, comprising 2,823 measures covering areas such as financial services, communications, housing, distribution, transport, energy, labour and education.

But it admitted that only 890 of the measures were new and the rest had already been cited in some form by various government ministries. It also left unclear the timing of when they would be implemented.
